Getting started with apsimR

Source: vignettes/apsimR.Rmd
apsimR.Rmd
library(apsimR)
has_apsim <- apsimR::apsim_available()

Why

An agronomist who already has an APSIM Next Generation file open asks one question before anything else: can I drive this simulator from R, get back a result with enough provenance that a causal or decision tool downstream can trust it, and will my analysis still tell me something useful, rather than simply fail, on a laptop where APSIM itself is not installed? This vignette answers all three parts of that question by walking every verb apsimR exposes: reading and running a simulation, fitting a reduced-form mechanism to its output, building the shared forward-model closure that calibration, sensitivity analysis and emulation all reduce to, validating simulated output against observations, generating a known-causal-structure dataset to grade a causal method against, and handing every result on into the orchestra’s shared manifest contract.

What

apsim_sim() reads an .apsimx file into a typed object that round-trips through apsim_write(); apsim_available(), apsim_version() and apsim_configure() report and control what simulator apsimR finds, and every verb that needs the simulator returns a typed apsim_abstention (checked with is_apsim_abstention()) rather than an error when it is absent. apsim_predict() runs the simulator once and returns its report as a predictions manifest; apsim_estimate() runs it across a varying input and fits an interpretable dose-response to the result. Calibration, sensitivity analysis and emulation are the same operation seen three ways – vary parameters, run the simulator, reduce each run to an observation vector – so all three are built over one shared closure, apsim_forward_model(), fed by parameter points from apsim_design(): apsim_calibrate() solves the inverse problem (which parameters reproduce observed data), apsim_sensitivity() ranks which parameters drive an output, and apsim_emulate() fits a fast Gaussian-process surrogate for one. apsim_validate() scores simulated output against observations with typed goodness-of-fit metrics, and apsim_ground_truth() uses the simulator’s ability to reveal both potential outcomes of the same unit to manufacture a dataset with a known causal answer, for grading a causal method that could never see that answer from a real experiment. Every verb returns an apsim_manifest; as_orchestra_manifest() and as_pesto_manifest() carry that result into the wider orchestra.

Do

Is the simulator available, and what happens when it is not?

apsimR is standalone-functional: it installs and loads with no simulator present, and every simulator-dependent verb abstains, returning a typed reason, rather than erroring, when APSIM is absent.

apsim_available()
#> [1] FALSE
apsim_version()
#> [1] NA

When the simulator cannot be found, a verb returns an apsim_abstention a caller can branch on. The demonstration below deliberately points apsimR at a non-existent Models executable to force that path, then reverts to auto-discovery.

# A minimal simulation file, and a deliberately wrong simulator path.
f <- tempfile(fileext = ".apsimx")
writeLines(paste0('{"$type":"Models.Core.Simulations, Models",',
                  '"Name":"Simulations","Children":[]}'), f)
apsim_configure(models = file.path(tempdir(), "no-such-Models"))

res <- apsim_predict(f)
is_apsim_abstention(res)
#> [1] TRUE
res$reason
#> [1] "runtime_unavailable"

apsim_configure() # revert to auto-discovery

Reading a simulation file

An .apsimx file is a typed tree of model nodes. apsim_sim() reads it; the object round-trips through apsim_write(). Reading needs no simulator run, but the object records the installed APSIM version, so this section still depends on has_apsim.

APSIM Next Generation is not available on this build, so the shipped Wheat example is not read here; apsim_sim() itself needs no simulator run, but the section above shows the abstention every simulator-dependent verb falls back to instead.

Prediction

apsim_predict() runs the simulator and returns the simulated reports as a predictions manifest – a contract-shaped object carrying the outputs plus provenance (the APSIM version, an integrity hash).

APSIM Next Generation is not available on this build, so no prediction is run here; apsim_predict() would return the same typed abstention demonstrated above.

Estimation: fitting a reduced-form mechanism

apsim_estimate() runs the simulator across an input and fits a reduced-form mechanism (a saturating Mitscherlich dose-response by default), returning the fitted parameters as a parameters manifest – the interpretable summary a causal or decision member consumes. The default form is the classical saturating N-response curve attributed to Mitscherlich (1909),

y(x)=y0+ymax(1−e−rx),y(x) = y_0 + y_{\max}\left(1 - e^{-r x}\right),

with asymptote ymaxy_{\max}, zero-input intercept y0y_0 and curvature rr governing how quickly the response saturates (the Limits section below notes how this attribution was checked). apsim_estimate() fits this form by nonlinear least squares through the internal helper it calls, apsimR:::.apsim_fit_response(), which is what runs underneath every apsim_estimate(sim, x, y) call once the simulator is available. The demonstration below drives that helper directly on a synthetic N-response, so it needs no simulator run:

set.seed(1)
n_rate <- seq(0, 200, by = 10)
yield <- 1.1 + 4.2 * (1 - exp(-0.018 * n_rate)) +
  stats::rnorm(length(n_rate), 0, 0.1)
est_params <- apsimR:::.apsim_fit_response(n_rate, yield,
                                           response = "mitscherlich")
est_m <- apsim_manifest("parameters", "demo", params = est_params)
Mitscherlich parameters fitted to the synthetic N-response demonstration.
ymax rate y0
4.259 0.018 1.072

The forward model: one machine for three verbs

Calibration, sensitivity analysis and emulation are the same operation seen three ways – vary some APSIM parameters, run the simulator, reduce each run to a small observation vector. apsim_forward_model() builds that operation once, as a closure of the orchestra-standard shape function(theta) -> obs: theta is an nreal x npar matrix (one row per parameter set), obs an nreal x nobs matrix. A single APSIM invocation per row applies the edits and runs the file in one --apply config; failed runs become NA rows rather than aborting the sweep. Building the closure and calling it are two different costs – building is free, but calling it runs the simulator once per row, so the call below is shown for its shape only and is not evaluated in this render (see the note after the design table for why).

fm <- apsim_forward_model(
  apsim_example("Wheat"),
  parm_paths = "[Fertilise at sowing].Script.Amount",
  output = "Yield")
fm(matrix(c(0, 100, 200), ncol = 1L)) # three nitrogen rates -> three yields

apsim_design() builds the parameter points a sweep evaluates – a space-filling Latin hypercube by default. It is pure (no simulator), so it runs anywhere:

d_design <- apsim_design(
  c("[Sow].Script.Population", "[Fertilise].Amount"),
  lower = c(50, 0), upper = c(200, 200), n = 5L, seed = 1L)
A five-point Latin-hypercube design over two parameters.
[Sow].Script.Population [Fertilise].Amount
176.2 167.1
70.6 135.4
103.1 99.9
131.5 39.7
151.4 71.1

The forward-model call above, and the calibration, sensitivity and full emulation demonstrations in the next three sections, each invoke the simulator many times over: a calibration ensemble alone runs it up to several hundred times. Even on a build where APSIM is installed, running all of that live inside this vignette would take much longer than its render-time budget allows, so those calls are shown for their shape only. Each function’s own help page carries a runnable example gated on apsim_available().

Calibration

apsim_calibrate() solves the inverse problem: find the parameters whose simulated observations best match data, over a box. The optim backend returns a bounded least-squares point estimate with no extra dependency; the ies backend (default when PESTO is installed) returns a posterior parameter ensemble through an iterative ensemble smoother, with RTPS inflation guarding against ensemble collapse. Several targets calibrate jointly through one weighted misfit.

apsim_calibrate(
  apsim_example("Wheat"),
  parm_paths = "[Fertilise at sowing].Script.Amount",
  lower = 0, upper = 250,
  observed = c(Yield = 2200), output = "Yield",
  backend = "ies", n_real = 50L, seed = 1L)

Sensitivity analysis

apsim_sensitivity() asks which inputs drive an output. Morris screening (the default) ranks factors by mean absolute elementary effect (mu_star) at a cost of r(p + 1) runs and flags interaction or non-linearity (sigma); the Sobol-Jansen method decomposes the output variance into first-order (S) and total (T) indices at a higher cost of n(p + 2) runs. Both use the sensitivity package over the same forward model.

apsim_sensitivity(
  apsim_example("Wheat"),
  parm_paths = c("[Fertilise at sowing].Script.Amount",
                "[Sow using a variable rule].Script.Population"),
  lower = c(0, 50), upper = c(250, 200),
  output = "Yield", method = "morris", morris_r = 10L, seed = 1L)

Emulation

A single APSIM run costs seconds; a sweep needs thousands. apsim_emulate() runs the simulator at a space-filling design once, fits a Gaussian-process surrogate, then predicts anywhere in microseconds with a calibrated uncertainty. Every emulator is returned with mandatory leave-one-out diagnostics: a surrogate with no measure of its own reliability is worse than none. The default backend is a genuine exact GP with an automatic-relevance-determination (ARD) squared-exponential kernel,

k(x,x′)=σf2exp⁡(−12∑j=1p(xj−xj′)2ℓj2)+σn2𝟙[x=x′],k(x, x') = \sigma_f^2 \exp\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{p} \frac{(x_j - x_j')^2}{\ell_j^2}\right) + \sigma_n^2 \,\mathbb{1}[x = x'],

with a per-dimension length-scale ℓj\ell_j, signal variance σf2\sigma_f^2 and noise variance σn2\sigma_n^2 all fitted by maximising the exact log marginal likelihood (Rasmussen and Williams, 2006, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning), not fixed by a heuristic. It needs no extra package and is exercised directly here (via the internal training/prediction pair apsimR:::.apsim_gp_train() / apsimR:::.apsim_gp_predict() that apsim_emulate() itself calls) on a one-dimensional test function, with a genuine leave-one-out pass – each point predicted from a GP refit on the other eleven – rather than a stand-in smoother:

set.seed(1)
truth <- function(x) sin(x) + 0.1 * x
xtr <- matrix(seq(0, 10, length.out = 12), ncol = 1L)
ytr <- truth(xtr[, 1L])

# A genuine leave-one-out pass: refit the GP on the other 11 points and
# predict the held-out one, for each point in turn.
loo <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(xtr)), function(i) {
  gp <- apsimR:::.apsim_gp_train(xtr[-i, , drop = FALSE], ytr[-i])
  pr <- apsimR:::.apsim_gp_predict(gp, xtr[i, , drop = FALSE])
  c(mean = pr$mean, sd = pr$sd)
}, numeric(2)))
loo_rmse <- sqrt(mean((ytr - loo[, "mean"])^2))
lo <- loo[, "mean"] - 1.96 * loo[, "sd"]
hi <- loo[, "mean"] + 1.96 * loo[, "sd"]
covered <- ytr >= lo & ytr <= hi
loo_df <- data.frame(
  x = xtr[, 1L], y_true = ytr, y_mean = loo[, "mean"], lo = lo, hi = hi,
  covered = ifelse(covered, "within 95% interval", "outside 95% interval"))
ggplot2::ggplot(loo_df, ggplot2::aes(x = x)) +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(ggplot2::aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi),
                       fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.5) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(y = y_mean), colour = "#0072B2") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(y = y_true, colour = covered), size = 2.6) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(
    name = NULL,
    values = c("within 95% interval" = "#009E73",
              "outside 95% interval" = "#D55E00")) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "x (arbitrary input units)", y = "y (arbitrary output units)",
    title = "Leave-one-out predictions from the exact GP",
    subtitle = sprintf("RMSE = %.3f | 95%% coverage = %d / %d points",
                       loo_rmse, sum(covered), length(covered))) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()

Leave-one-out predictions from the exact GP against the true test function, with the fitted 95% interval (shaded) and the GP mean (line). Point colour marks whether the truth fell inside its own held-out interval; the subtitle reports the RMSE and coverage count the caption below also interprets.

A single twelve-point draw is far too small to certify calibration either way; the reported coverage95 from a full apsim_emulate() run (typically evaluated over dozens of held-out points against a design of thirty or more) is the number to trust, and it can – and, on at least one independent Branin-function check, did – run below its nominal 95%, so read it rather than assume the interval is calibrated.

On the simulator the same idea fits an emulator of yield against nitrogen, with apsim_emulate() reporting the leave-one-out RMSE, R-squared and 95% coverage, and predict() emulating new rates. Like the calibration and sensitivity calls above, running this against the real simulator costs thirty APSIM invocations, so it is shown for its shape only:

em <- apsim_emulate(
  apsim_example("Wheat"),
  parm_paths = "[Fertilise at sowing].Script.Amount",
  lower = 0, upper = 250, output = "Yield", n = 30L, seed = 1L)
em                                       # prints the LOO diagnostics
predict(em, matrix(c(75, 175), ncol = 1L))

Validation

apsim_validate() confronts simulated output with observations and reports the standard agronomic goodness-of-fit metrics – error magnitude (RMSE, MAE), direction (mean error, percent bias) and skill relative to the observed mean (Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency, Willmott’s index of agreement, RSR) – with a typed verdict against the performance bands of Moriasi et al. (2007). It accepts an apsim_predict() manifest, a data frame (optionally joined to the observations on a key such as date), or plain vectors:

observed <- c(2.1, 3.4, 4.0, 5.2, 6.1)
simulated <- c(2.0, 3.6, 3.8, 5.1, 5.9)
v <- apsim_validate(simulated, observed)
Goodness-of-fit metrics for the five-point validation demonstration (verdict: very good).
n me mae rmse nse r2 d rsr pbias
5 -0.08 0.16 0.167 0.986 0.99 0.996 0.107 -1.923

An observed-versus-predicted plot is available through apsim_validation_plot() when ggplot2 is installed:

apsim_validation_plot(v)

Simulated against observed values for the five-point demonstration pair, with the 1:1 line of perfect agreement. Points close to the line and on both sides of it (rather than all above or all below) indicate no systematic bias, consistent with the near-zero percent bias reported in the table above.

Ground truth: APSIM as a causal test-bench

A real experiment never observes both potential outcomes of the same unit, so the true causal effect is unknowable and a causal method can only be trusted, never scored. A process simulator escapes that: run the same unit under control and under treatment and both outcomes are known. apsim_ground_truth() does this across heterogeneous units to manufacture an observing-system simulation experiment (OSSE) – a dataset of observed (covariates, treatment, outcome) whose true individual and average treatment effects are recorded alongside. Treatment can be assigned at random, or confounded by a covariate that also moves the outcome, so a causal member (such as the orchestra’s kernR tools) can be handed the observed data and graded against the truth it cannot see. Each unit needs two simulator runs (one per potential outcome), so this demonstration is also shown for its shape only:

units <- data.frame(
  `[Sow using a variable rule].Script.Population` = c(80, 120, 160, 200),
  check.names = FALSE)
gt <- apsim_ground_truth(
  apsim_example("Wheat"),
  treatment = "[Fertilise at sowing].Script.Amount",
  control = 0, treated = 150, units = units, output = "Yield",
  assignment = "confounded",
  confounder = "[Sow using a variable rule].Script.Population", seed = 1L)

gt                   # prints the true ATE and the (biased) naive difference
head(gt@observed)    # (covariates, W, Y) -- the input to a causal method
gt@truth$ate         # the answer key

Under confounding the naive treatment-minus-control difference is biased away from gt@truth$ate; a causal method that conditions on the covariates should recover the recorded ATE. That recovery is the validation gate for the orchestra’s causal members.

Composing with the orchestra

Every result-returning verb produces an apsim_manifest, a versioned, provenance-complete object of its own. Two adapters carry it into the wider orchestra.

as_orchestra_manifest() emits the federation’s general result contract (orchestra_manifest, contract C2 v2 in ORCHESTRA.md) at schema 2.0.0-draft, and is the route for any apsimR result. A prediction stays a prediction, a sensitivity table becomes a statement about parameters, and an emulator or a validation becomes a statement about predictions – with the original apsimR target preserved in the manifest’s metadata and a validation verdict lifted into the contract’s typed summary slot. verify_manifest() recomputes the payload hash, so a consumer detects a manifest whose payload was modified after emission. The hash recipe itself is tested against an independently authored sibling implementation (optimix) in the package’s own test suite, which this vignette does not repeat.

om <- as_orchestra_manifest(v)
om
#> <orchestra_manifest>
#>   schema:   2.0.0-draft
#>   emitter:  apsimR 0.3.2.9000
#>   target:   predictions
#>   method:   apsim:validate
#>   run_id:   apsimR-8124ba10b764
#>   verdict:  very good
#>   outputs:  5 rows x 2 cols
#>   hash:     sha256:8124ba10b76475f322f9bffeadb3776a15ca0c35f2c2a9db2591a98a3572e63f

as_pesto_manifest() bridges into PESTO’s narrower C2 ensemble contract (pesto_ensemble_manifest), which carries a parameter ensemble alongside the row-aligned simulated observations that ensemble produced. Exactly one apsimR result is an object of that kind – the posterior ensemble from apsim_calibrate(backend = "ies"), which PESTO’s own ensemble smoother produced. Every other result abstains with a typed reason naming the requirement it does not meet and pointing back at as_orchestra_manifest(), rather than being forced into slots it has no basis to fill.

Read

APSIM Next Generation is not installed on this build, so every simulator-dependent section above took the abstention path instead of a real run – the same path the deliberately-broken configuration demonstrates directly.

apsim_available() reports FALSE on the machine that rendered this copy of the vignette, and the deliberately-misconfigured call above abstains with reason runtime_unavailable, exactly the reason a genuinely APSIM-less build would report from every simulator-dependent verb. The fitted Mitscherlich curve on the synthetic N-response demonstration recovers an asymptote of 4.26, a curvature of 0.0182 and a zero-input intercept of 1.07, against the generating values 4.2, 0.018 and 1.1 used to build the synthetic data above – close enough, on this one draw, to show the fit recovers the generating mechanism rather than merely interpolating it. The Latin hypercube design table spans both parameters’ full ranges (population 50 to 200, fertiliser amount 0 to 200) at its five requested points, which is what a space-filling design over a box is meant to do at even a handful of points.

On the twelve-point leave-one-out demonstration, every held-out point sits close to its own leave-one-out prediction (RMSE 0.007), and the shaded 95% interval covers the truth at 12 of 12 points, exactly as the figure’s colour split shows.

The validation demonstration grades a five-point synthetic pair as very good (Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency 0.99, RMSE 0.167, percent bias -1.9), and the figure shows why: the points sit close to the 1:1 line on both sides of it rather than uniformly above or below, consistent with a percent bias close to zero.

Lifting that validation result through as_orchestra_manifest() produces a manifest whose integrity check passes (verify_manifest(om)$ok is TRUE) and whose headline verdict, very good, matches the validation’s own typed grade above – the contract’s typed summary slot is not a re-derivation, it is the same verdict carried into a shape every other orchestra member can read without knowing apsimR’s own vocabulary.

Taken together, the answer to the opening question is yes on all three counts: apsimR drives APSIM from R, returns results with enough provenance (a hashed, versioned manifest) for a downstream member to trust, and, on a build without the simulator, every one of those same verbs abstains with a typed reason rather than failing outright, as the abstention demonstration above shows directly.

Limits

This vignette runs one real simulator call, if APSIM is installed, and otherwise demonstrates the abstention path a real run would fall back on; the calibration, sensitivity, full emulation and ground-truth sections show only the shape of a call whose simulator cost (from dozens to several hundred APSIM invocations) does not fit this vignette’s render-time budget, even on a build where the simulator is present – each function’s own help page carries a runnable, simulator-gated example instead. The twelve-point leave-one-out demonstration is a small synthetic illustration, not a calibration certificate: coverage measured on twelve points is not a meaningful diagnostic on its own, and the text above says so explicitly before quoting a number from it. The Moriasi et al. (2007) verdict bands were derived for monthly watershed and streamflow simulation, not paddock-scale crop yield, and the typed grade in metadata$verdict reads Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency alone; the RMSE and percent bias reported in the same table are worth reading alongside it rather than trusting the single label. The Mitscherlich (1909) attribution for the saturating dose-response form, and the Rasmussen and Williams (2006) attribution for the exact-GP formulation, are both cited from the literature record; neither citation was checked against its original source in this pass, so the historical attribution should be read as indicative rather than bibliographically confirmed. The ground-truth demonstration illustrates the mechanism – a confounded assignment biases a naive comparison away from the recorded average treatment effect – without itself running; grading a causal method against apsimR’s OSSE output, the validation gate the Do section describes, is not exercised here. The exact-GP backend’s anisotropic fit has been checked elsewhere against a reference implementation (DiceKriging), a comparison this vignette does not repeat.

What to read next

The package’s function reference lists every verb this vignette does not have room to run for real, each documented with its own runnable, simulator-gated example. Getting Started with PESTO introduces the iterative ensemble smoother that apsim_calibrate(backend = "ies") delegates to. Getting started with decideR walks the decision layer that reads the orchestra_manifest this vignette’s final section builds.

Reproduce

Seed 1 for the synthetic N-response, the Latin-hypercube design, the leave-one-out demonstration and the calibration/sensitivity/emulation call shapes shown above. Package versions and the APSIM version this copy was rendered against follow.
